title: The midwives (Exodus 1:15–21)
hookLine: Shiphrah and Puah refuse to kill the boys; they feared God more than Pharaoh

lines: IF IT'S A SON, KILL HIM.
cards: Forced labor hasn't worked; the Israelites keep growing. So the king tries something worse, and quieter. He calls in two midwives, the women who sit with mothers in labor and catch the babies.
His order: when you deliver a Hebrew woman, look. If it's a son, kill him. If it's a daughter, let her live.

A death at a birth could pass for natural. It's an order given in private by the king of Egypt to two women with no power at all. And the Bible, which never tells us this Pharaoh's name, tells us theirs.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "the name of the one was Shiphrah, and the name of the other Puah."
Then the sentence that makes them unforgettable: "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive." Here, that fear isn't panic.
It's knowing whose word counts for more than the king's. The king calls them back: why have you let the boys live? They have an answer ready.
The Hebrew women aren't like Egyptian women, they say. They're lively; the babies are born before we even get there. Was it true, or a clever excuse?
The text doesn't say, and readers, Christian and Jewish, still debate it.

What it does say is that God dealt well with them, and gave them households of their own. The Hebrew can be read as Hebrew midwives or as midwives to the Hebrews, so we don't know for certain which people they came from.
Some ancient Jewish teachers thought they were Moses's own mother and sister. What we do know is that the story of the way out begins with two women saying no.

teach.h: AND SAVED THE MEN CHILDREN ALIVE.
teach.b: Not with an army, not with a prophet: with two professionals quietly refusing to do harm. This week was full of people choosing: Judah to stay instead of the boy, Joseph not to take revenge, Jacob to go.
And now, at the start of a new book, Shiphrah and Puah choose life.

how: Christians and Jews tell the story of Shiphrah and Puah as an example of refusing an unjust order, and the two are named in sermons on conscience and courage.

games.q: what's inside the refusal — tap the pairs.
p: the midwives, named by the text
the king said: let them live
their answer about the Hebrew women

s: the king ordered the midwives to kill the girls too
only the boys: if it be a daughter, then she shall live.

games.q: you're a midwife. the king of Egypt himself orders you, in private, to kill every Hebrew boy you deliver. what do you do?
o: refuse quietly, and let the boys live.
run away from Egypt that night.
games.why: "the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive."

practice: Say to yourself the name of someone who refused to go along with something they knew was wrong: a nurse, a teacher, a coworker, a grandparent, a stranger in a story you once heard.
Maybe nobody thanked them, or even knew; name them anyway, the way the Bible names Shiphrah and Puah. If you pray, you can give thanks for them; if you don't, honor them in your heart.

wordCard.voice: The midwives. Shiphrah and Puah, who were ordered by Pharaoh to kill the Hebrew baby boys, feared God, and let them live.

orig.note: Hebrew: Shiphrah, one of the two midwives the text names, while the king stays nameless.

carryVoice: Your line: two women said no. The Bible kept both their names. See you tomorrow.
